title: Airbnb Smart Pricing and racial revenue gap (Zhang, Mehta, Singh, Srinivasan)
author_source: Shunyuan Zhang, Nitin Mehta, Param Vir Singh, Kannan Srinivasan; Marketing Science 40(5), 2021, 'Frontiers: Can an Artificial Intelligence Algorithm Mitigate Racial Economic Inequality? An Analysis in the Context of Airbnb', research article
note: Airbnb's Smart Pricing algorithm suggests nightly prices to hosts. Hosts who adopted it increased revenue, and among adopters the revenue gap between white and Black hosts shrank substantially, but Black hosts were less likely to adopt, so the overall gap could widen. Shows algorithmic pricing benefits and distributional effects. Technical background: Ye et al. (KDD 2018) 'Customized Regression Model for Airbnb Dynamic Pricing'.
course_use: Discussion on algorithmic pricing and fairness; paid journal (WU-Lizenz via INFORMS likely)

title: The Economist subscription decoy (Ariely)
author_source: Dan Ariely, 'Predictably Irrational', HarperCollins 2008, chapter 1, book example (MIT student experiment)
note: Offer: web-only USD 59, print-only USD 125, print+web USD 125. With the dominated print-only decoy, 84% of 100 MIT students chose print+web and 16% web-only; without the decoy, 68% chose web-only and 32% print+web. Illustrates the decoy/asymmetric dominance effect in price architecture. Caveat: small classroom sample; replications show weaker effects.
course_use: Run the same choice live in class with two groups (online poll) before revealing the results. Book (paid); free summaries exist

title: J.C. Penney 'Fair and Square' pricing failure (2012-2013)
author_source: J.C. Penney annual report 2012; documented in HBS case 513036 (Ofek, Avery)
note: Replacing hundreds of promotions per year with everyday prices and three tiers led to roughly a 25% decline in 2012 sales (about USD 4bn) and CEO Ron Johnson's dismissal in April 2013; coupons and 'sales' returned. Shows that consumers value the transaction utility of deals, not just low final prices (Thaler).
course_use: Warm-up: show old and new price tags and ask which shoppers prefer. Free news coverage; case paid

title: Coca-Cola temperature-sensitive vending machines (1999) and Spain's Minute Maid machine (2012-2013)
author_source: Tampa Bay Times archive, 'Coke tests vending machine that alters price', 28 October 1999, news article
note: CEO Douglas Ivester said it was 'fair' that a cold drink should cost more on hot days; public backlash followed and Coca-Cola said the technology was not deployed. In contrast, a 2012-2013 Minute Maid campaign in Spain used machines that lowered prices as temperature rose (approx. USD 1.20 above 86F vs. USD 2.40 at cooler temperatures). Same mechanism, opposite framing.
course_use: Classic framing/fairness example for a dynamic pricing lecture. Free

title: Apple iPhone launch price cut and USD 100 credit (2007)
author_source: Apple; documented in Darden case UV1228; Wikipedia overview
note: The 8GB iPhone launched at USD 599 in June 2007; about two months later Apple cut it to USD 399. After early-adopter anger, Steve Jobs offered a USD 100 Apple Store credit. Illustrates price skimming, intertemporal price discrimination and reference-price fairness.
course_use: Warm-up on skimming; discuss whether the credit was necessary. Free

title: Tesla price cuts (2023) and margin effects
author_source: Tesla Investor Relations, quarterly updates 2023, company information
note: From January 2023 Tesla cut prices repeatedly (e.g. Model Y in the US by up to about 20%), boosting volume and squeezing rivals but reducing automotive gross margin, and angering recent buyers in China who protested at showrooms. Illustrates price as a competitive weapon, cost-down pass-through and price-protection expectations.
course_use: Discussion: when is a price war rational for a cost leader? Free (verify figures in Q4 2022/Q1 2023 updates)

title: Costco hot dog and soda combo at USD 1.50 since 1985
author_source: Costco Wholesale; statements by CFO in earnings calls (2024), news coverage
note: Costco has kept its hot dog and soda combo at USD 1.50 since 1985 despite inflation; co-founder Jim Sinegal reportedly told the CEO 'if you raise the price of the hot dog, I will kill you'. Loss-leader / price image tool supporting the membership model (fees raised in 2024 to USD 65). Illustrates price image and signalling.
course_use: Warm-up on price image and loss leaders. Free (anecdote; verify quotes)

title: Starbucks price increases and traffic decline (2024)
author_source: Starbucks Corporation, Q4 FY2024 earnings release, company information
note: After several years of price increases, Starbucks reported falling US comparable transactions in 2024 (Q4 FY2024 US comparable store sales down about 6% with transactions down about 10%); the new CEO Brian Niccol's 'Back to Starbucks' plan paused further price increases and simplified the menu. Illustrates the limits of price-led revenue growth when perceived value falls.
course_use: Discussion: price elasticity in premium FMCG/food service. Free (verify figures in earnings release)

title: Carrefour shrinkflation labels (France, 2023) and French labelling decree (2024)
author_source: Carrefour France, September 2023; French government decree on shrinkflation information, in force July 2024, news/regulation
note: In September 2023 Carrefour put shelf labels on a few dozen branded products whose pack sizes shrank while prices stayed or rose, to pressure suppliers in negotiations. France then required retailers to inform consumers about shrinkflation from July 2024. Illustrates hidden price increases, unit pricing and retailer-supplier power.
course_use: Warm-up: bring two packs; compute unit price change. Free (verify exact count of labelled products)

title: Austrian food sector inquiry (BWB Branchenuntersuchung Lebensmittel)
author_source: Bundeswettbewerbsbehörde (BWB), Austria, sector inquiry food retail, 2023 reports, regulator
note: During the 2022-2023 inflation peak the Austrian competition authority examined price formation along the food supply chain, high retail concentration (Rewe/Billa, Spar, Hofer and Lidl together hold roughly 90% of grocery retail), shrinkflation and price differences vs. Germany. Recommended more price transparency (price-comparison databases). Local example for pricing power and retail margins.
course_use: Local case for discussion on price fairness and concentration (German-language sources). Free; locate the exact report on bwb.gv.at

title: 'Österreich-Aufschlag': territorial supply constraints and higher prices in Austria
author_source: Austrian government, Arbeiterkammer and EU Commission debate on territorial supply constraints, 2024-2025, policy/news
note: Identical branded products often cost more in Austria than in Germany; manufacturers use territorial supply constraints to prevent Austrian retailers from buying cheaper in Germany. Austria pushed the EU Commission to act. Illustrates international price discrimination, arbitrage prevention and fences.
course_use: Discussion on cross-border price discrimination in the EU single market. Free (German-language sources; verify current status)

title: OEBB Sparschiene contingent-based train pricing
author_source: Austrian Federal Railways (OEBB), company information
note: OEBB sells limited contingents of discounted 'Sparschiene' tickets (domestic and to neighbouring countries) from low entry prices, train-specific and non-refundable; prices step up as contingents sell out, while flexible standard fares remain. A local example of airline-style revenue management with fences (train binding, no refunds). Contrast with KlimaTicket flat-rate pricing.
course_use: Exercise: students compare Sparschiene prices for the same route at different booking horizons. Free (verify current entry prices)

title: KlimaTicket Oesterreich flat-rate pricing and price increases
author_source: KlimaTicket Oe (One Mobility GmbH / Austrian Ministry), official website
note: Austria-wide annual public transport ticket launched October 2021 (Classic EUR 1,095). Prices: Classic EUR 1,300 from 1 Aug 2025 and EUR 1,400 from 1 Jan 2026; Jugend/Senior/Spezial EUR 1,050 from 2026; earlier 7.7% increase on 1 Jan 2025; family option EUR 140 per year. Illustrates flat-rate pricing, segment discounts and political/indexation-based price adjustments.
course_use: Local exercise: break-even number of trips vs. single tickets; discussion of flat-rate bias. Free

title: Wiener Linien Jahreskarte: from EUR 365 to EUR 467
author_source: Wiener Linien, official Jahreskarte page
note: Vienna's annual pass cost EUR 365 ('one euro a day') from 2012 to 2025, a famous anchor and policy symbol; the current price is EUR 467 one-off (EUR 461 digital) or EUR 506.40 via monthly direct debit, reduced fares EUR 294-300. Shows a long-held psychological price point, its political value and the shock when it is abandoned; also instalment surcharges.
course_use: Local warm-up: was 'EUR 1 per day' worth defending? Free

title: Deutschlandticket price path (EUR 49 to 58 to 63)
author_source: German federal and state transport ministers, Deutschlandticket decisions, policy/news
note: Germany's nationwide public transport subscription launched in May 2023 at EUR 49 per month, rose to EUR 58 in January 2025 and EUR 63 in January 2026 after political negotiation over subsidies. Useful comparison with KlimaTicket on price elasticity of transit demand and subscription churn after increases.
course_use: Comparative example DACH region. Free (verify 2026 price)

title: Austrian telecom price indexation and 'Servicepauschale' rulings (A1, Magenta, Drei)
author_source: Austrian Supreme Court (OGH) rulings and Arbeiterkammer/VKI actions on telecom fees and index clauses, 2023-2024, legal/news
note: Austrian mobile operators used annual CPI-linked price increases and annual 'Servicepauschale' fees; courts and consumer groups challenged these clauses, and operators adjusted contracts. Illustrates drip pricing, partitioned pricing and legal limits on unilateral price changes.
course_use: Discussion on partitioned pricing and price transparency in contracts. Free (German-language; verify specific rulings)

title: Red Bull premium pricing
author_source: Red Bull GmbH; trade press and brand-strategy literature
note: Red Bull has kept a price premium over Coca-Cola and private-label energy drinks since its 1987 Austrian launch, with a single 250 ml can price point and no promotional discounting, supporting a premium brand image built on events and media rather than price. Illustrates prestige pricing and price as a positioning signal (Austrian example).
course_use: Discussion: what fences protect a premium price against cheap imitators (e.g. Hofer/Lidl private labels)? Free (anecdotal; collect current shelf prices)

title: Slack Fair Billing Policy
author_source: Slack Technologies (Salesforce), Help Center article, company information
note: Slack bills only for active paid members: a member counts as inactive after 28 days of no use and Slack automatically credits the unused part of the billing period; reactivations are prorated. A seat-based SaaS price metric adjusted towards usage to increase perceived fairness and reduce purchase risk.
course_use: SaaS price-metric discussion (seat vs. active user vs. usage). Free

title: Zoom freemium 40-minute limit
author_source: Zoom Video Communications, pricing page, company information
note: Zoom's free plan limits group meetings to 40 minutes; paid plans remove the limit. The time limit is a fence that lets free users experience value while creating a natural upgrade trigger for regular group meetings. Illustrates freemium fence design.
course_use: Warm-up on freemium fences; compare with Dropbox storage caps. Free

title: OpenAI ChatGPT Plus and Pro pricing
author_source: OpenAI, ChatGPT pricing page and announcements (Plus Feb 2023, Pro Dec 2024), company information
note: ChatGPT Plus launched at USD 20 per month (February 2023) and Pro at USD 200 per month (December 2024); Sam Altman said in January 2025 that Pro was losing money because usage was higher than expected. Lower-priced plans (e.g. ChatGPT Go, launched first in India) followed. Illustrates good-better-best tiers, unlimited-usage risk with variable costs, and regional pricing.
course_use: Discussion on pricing products with high variable (compute) costs; link to IESE OpenAI case I00343. Free (page blocked automated fetch; verify current plans)

title: GitHub Copilot plans and AI-credit metering
author_source: GitHub, Copilot plans page, company information
note: Individual plans: Free, Pro USD 10, Pro+ USD 39, Max USD 100 per month, each including a dollar-denominated allowance of GitHub AI Credits (1 credit = USD 0.01) plus a flex allotment; code completions are unlimited and do not use credits; paid plans can buy additional usage. Shows the shift from flat subscriptions to hybrid subscription-plus-usage pricing for AI.
course_use: Exercise: which plan is optimal for three developer personas? Free

title: Salesforce Agentforce pricing: per conversation, per action, per user
author_source: Salesforce, Agentforce pricing page, company information
note: Three coexisting models: USD 2 per customer-facing conversation; Flex Credits at USD 500 per 100,000 credits (a standard action = 20 credits, about USD 0.10); per-user add-ons at USD 125 per user per month (Industries USD 150; Agentforce User Licence USD 5 plus credits). Illustrates choice of price metric (outcome proxy vs. usage vs. seats) for AI agents.
course_use: Compare with Intercom Fin; ask which metric best tracks customer value. Free

title: Intercom Fin outcome-based pricing (USD 0.99 per outcome)
author_source: Intercom, pricing page, company information
note: Fin AI agent costs USD 0.99 per outcome, counted when a customer confirms resolution, stops asking for help after Fin's answer, or Fin completes a workflow; helpdesk seats cost USD 29 / 85 / 132 per month. A prominent example of outcome-based pricing aligning price with customer value, but with measurement and incentive questions.
course_use: Discussion: what counts as an 'outcome' and who bears the risk? Links to Michelin and Rolls-Royce B2B cases. Free

title: Microsoft 365 price increase with Copilot bundled (2025)
author_source: Microsoft, consumer announcements January 2025, company information
note: In January 2025 Microsoft added Copilot AI to Microsoft 365 Personal and Family and raised prices (US by USD 3 per month), while offering 'Classic' plans without Copilot at the old price for existing subscribers. Illustrates forced bundling, opt-out defaults and status quo bias in subscription price increases.
course_use: Warm-up: would you switch to Classic? Discuss defaults. Free (verify exact figures and EU prices)

title: Radiohead 'In Rainbows' pay-what-you-want release (2007)
author_source: Radiohead; comScore estimates reported in news, October-November 2007
note: Radiohead let fans download 'In Rainbows' at any price they chose. comScore estimated that about 38% of downloaders paid, with an average of about USD 6 per paying download (more in the US); the band later released a physical CD and box set at fixed prices. Illustrates pay-what-you-want, voluntary payments and versioning.
course_use: Warm-up on PWYW; follow with a quick in-class PWYW experiment. Free (estimates disputed by the band)

title: Humble Bundle pay-what-you-want with charity split
author_source: Humble Bundle (now IGN), company information
note: Game and e-book bundles sold at pay-what-you-want prices, with buyers choosing how to split payment between developers, charity and Humble; paying above the average unlocks extra items, turning the average price into a public reference point and a threshold. Illustrates PWYW with anchors and social preferences.
course_use: Discussion: how do the 'beat the average' tier and charity split raise payments? Free

title: Pay-what-you-want field experiment with charity (Gneezy et al., Science 2010)
author_source: Ayelet Gneezy, Uri Gneezy, Leif D. Nelson, Amber Brown; Science 329(5989), 2010, 'Shared Social Responsibility: A Field Experiment in Pay-What-You-Want Pricing and Charitable Giving', research article
note: Field experiment with about 113,000 amusement-park ride photos: pay-what-you-want combined with a 50% charity donation increased uptake and profits compared with fixed prices or PWYW alone. Shows that social preferences shape WTP under voluntary pricing.
course_use: Evidence slide after the Radiohead/Humble examples; exam question on PWYW design. Paid journal (WU-Lizenz via Science likely)

title: Dollar Shave Club vs. Gillette pricing (USD 1 razor subscription)
author_source: Paddle / ProfitWell pricing teardown 'Dollar Shave Club and Gillette pricing', company blog
note: Dollar Shave Club's viral 2012 launch video and USD 1 per month entry offer undercut Gillette's premium blade pricing; Unilever bought DSC for about USD 1bn in 2016 and Gillette cut prices in 2017. The teardown, based on a survey of 6,441 current, former or prospective customers, argues that heavy shavers were willing to pay much more than either company charged. Illustrates penetration pricing, subscriptions and the razor-blade model.
course_use: Discussion on disruption via price and the risk of leaving money on the table. Free (vendor blog; interpret survey with care)

title: Booking.com large-scale experimentation culture
author_source: Stefan Thomke, 'Building a Culture of Experimentation', Harvard Business Review, March-April 2020, article; Booking.com tech blog
note: Booking.com runs more than 1,000 concurrent online experiments and lets any employee launch tests; the article describes how A/B testing (including messaging, prices and display) is governed at scale. Context for using randomised experiments to measure price response, and the ethical guardrails needed for price tests.
course_use: Reading for a session on price experimentation vs. survey-based WTP. HBR article (paywall; WU library access via EBSCO likely)

title: Uber Engineering: building an intelligent experimentation platform
author_source: Zhenyu Zhao, Eva Feng; Uber Engineering Blog, 4 May 2017, company blog
note: Describes Uber's experimentation platform: staged rollouts, sequential testing (SLRT with jackknife variance cut false positives to about 5% vs. over 30% with a naive test) and flexible metric analysis. Not pricing-specific, but shows the infrastructure firms like Uber use to test price and feature changes and why naive A/B tests mislead with correlated user data.
course_use: Advanced/analytics students: discuss pitfalls of price A/B tests (peeking, correlated sessions). Free

title: Amazon/Apple e-book pricing: USD 9.99 vs. agency model (2010-2013)
author_source: US v. Apple Inc., US District Court SDNY, 2013 ruling; background in HBS cases 709486 and 710444
note: Amazon sold many Kindle e-books at USD 9.99, often below wholesale cost; with the 2010 iPad launch, five publishers and Apple moved to the agency model where publishers set retail prices (often USD 12.99-14.99). The DOJ sued in 2012 and the court found Apple liable for price-fixing in 2013. Illustrates channel pricing power, resale price control and antitrust limits.
course_use: Discussion on who should set the price in a channel; exam question on wholesale vs. agency. Free (verify DOJ page URL)

title: Disney theme parks dynamic date-based ticket pricing and Genie+/Lightning Lane
author_source: Walt Disney World / Disneyland; documented in Case Centre case 'The Genie Is Out of the Bottle' (2024)
note: Disney moved from flat park tickets to date-based dynamic pricing (2016 onward) and later monetised queue-skipping (Genie+ in 2021, replaced by Lightning Lane Multi Pass in 2024). Peak-day prices smooth demand; paid line-skipping raises fairness concerns. Illustrates peak-load pricing and unbundling of experience quality.
course_use: Discussion on peak pricing and perceived fairness; compare with Oasis. Free news coverage; case paid
